summary.text: Stephen Lynch is the Democratic U.S. Representative for Massachusetts's 8th District and won re-election on November 3, 2026.

A South Boston native, he worked as an ironworker and led his union before becoming a labor and employment attorney, a Massachusetts state legislator and, in 2001, a member of Congress. He sits on the House Financial Services and Oversight and Government Reform committees.

paragraphs.text: Lynch was born and raised in the public housing projects of South Boston, the son of an ironworker and a postal clerk, according to his official biography.
After graduating from South Boston High School in 1973, he entered the Ironworkers Apprenticeship Program and joined Ironworkers Local 7.

He worked as a structural ironworker for 18 years and was elected president of the union, which his office says made him the youngest president in its history; Ballotpedia says he took the post at age 30.
Studying nights and weekends, he earned a bachelor's degree in construction management from Wentworth Institute of Technology (1988, per Ballotpedia) and a law degree from Boston College (1991).
He was admitted to the Massachusetts and New Hampshire bars and worked as a labor and employment attorney.

Lynch was elected to the Massachusetts House of Representatives in 1994 and, after fourteen months, to the Massachusetts State Senate in a special election; in the Senate he chaired the Joint Committee on Commerce and Labor, and he served there until 2001.
He also earned a master's degree in public administration from Harvard's Kennedy School of Government in 1999.

He was first sworn in to the U.S. House in October 2001, following the death of Rep. John Joseph Moakley, and his office says his experience with plant closings as an ironworker led him to focus on U.S. trade policy.

In the 119th Congress, Lynch serves on the Financial Services Committee, where he is ranking member of the Subcommittee on Digital Assets, Financial Technology and Artificial Intelligence, and on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee.
He is a co-founder of the Congressional Labor and Working Families Caucus.
According to his official biography, he and his wife Margaret live in South Boston, where they raised their daughter Victoria and niece Crystal.
He won the November 3, 2026 general election with 69.4% of the vote to Robert Burke's 26.8% and Rasheed Walters's 3.8%, according to unofficial results reported by NBC News.
